text: Question three. What are continuous batching and PagedAttention? Batching lets one read of the weights serve many sequences at once. The catch is that answers end at different lengths. Static batching groups requests and waits until the longest one finishes, so the slots that finished early sit idle. Continuous batching, also called in-flight batching, admits a new request at any decode step, and releases a finished one immediately. In a simulation, eight slots work through a thousand requests whose answers run from ten to a thousand tokens, most of them short. Static batching keeps the slots busy thirty-seven percent of the time. Continuous batching, ninety-nine. Every busy slot needs cache memory, and no one knows in advance how long an answer will be. Reserve eight K tokens for a request that ends up using two thousand, and three quarters of its buffer sits empty. PagedAttention stores the cache in fixed-size blocks, the way an operating system pages memory, and hands out blocks as the answer grows. With blocks of sixteen tokens, the only waste is the unfilled end of a request's last block: under one percent of two thousand. And requests that share a prompt prefix can share its blocks. Less waste means more requests in the batch. PagedAttention came with vLLM, an open-source serving engine, whose paper reported two to four times the throughput of earlier systems at the same latency. Notice that last part. A bigger batch raises throughput while each user's tokens arrive more slowly, so a throughput number only means something at a stated latency. The last two levers make every byte read go further.
